Extractive desulfurization of model jet fuel using metal chloride modified deep eutectic solvents
Rupam Chatterjee a, Debarati Mitra a,* a Department of Chemical Technology, University of Calcutta, Kolkata 700009, India
ARTICLE INFO --- Keywords: Model jet fuel Desulfurization Deep eutectic solvents Solvent extraction Molecular dynamic simulation

ABSTRACT Crude oil contains various organic sulfur compounds comprising of heterocyclic and paraffinic hydrocarbons. During upgradation of crude oil, these sulfur compounds inevitably end up in the final products, which include different fuel fractions (gasoline, kerosene, diesel, etc.). Jet fuels are one such crude oil fraction. Combustion of high sulfur containing fuels lead to sulfur oxide emissions which is detrimental for the environment. Hydrodesulfurization (HDS) process is the conventional fuel desulfurization approach. However, this method is cost and energy intensive therefore, alternative desulfurization approaches are continually being investigated. One such fuel desulfurization route is solvent extraction utilizing deep eutectic solvents (DESs). In this investigation, a choline chloride and glycerol based DES has been formulated. Four different metal chlorides viz. iron(III) chloride, copper(II) chloride, zinc(II) chloride and tin(II) chloride were added to the DES with an objective to enhance the desulfurization efficiency. These solvents were characterized by FTIR, rheology, surface tension and Kamlet-Taft parameters. The effectiveness of these solvents towards desulfurization of model jet fuel has been analysed. A molecular dynamic simulation of the solvents as well as the model fuel has also been carried out for better understanding of the desulfurization process. Both the experimental and simulated findings indicated that the desulfurization efficiency of the DES containing copper(II) chloride was the maximum. The highest desulfurization efficiency of 99.15% (on total sulfur basis) with a solvent:feed ratio of 1:5 at an operating temperature of 25 °C and an extraction time of 3 h was achieved using the aforementioned DES.

1. Introduction Organic sulfur compounds are an integral part of petroleum distillates, including fuels. Jet fuel is no exception and untreated jet fuel can contain as high as 10,000 ppm of sulfur. Sulfur laden fuels when combusted in engines, lead to the emission of sulfur oxides (SOx), which eventually causes environmental pollution. Some of the undesirable effects of SOx pollution include acid rain, formation of obnoxious smog which can cause severe respiratory and cardiovascular problems in humans [1]. This has necessitated stringent measures from regulatory bodies all over the world to reduce the sulfur content in fuels, below a certain threshold [2]. In the case of jet fuels, the maximum permissible limit of sulfur is 3000 ppm since most of the emissions from jet fuel occur at high altitudes which have low impact on the environment. However, some of the jet emissions at lower altitudes, especially near airports could have detrimental effects. Also, this high sulfur content in jet fuels make them unsuitable for alternative applications viz. in fuel cells [3]. Hydrodesulfurization (HDS) utilizing NiMo/CoMo catalysts is the

stereotypical fuel desulfurization approach in refineries [4]. However, this process operates under high pressure and high temperature and utilizes expensive proprietary catalysts making itboth energy and cost intensive. Also, HDS process is not very efficient in removing hetero- cyclic sulfur compounds under standard operating conditions due to low reactivity of these compounds and higher severity (i.e. higher temper- ature and pressure) is required to remove these compounds [1,2,4,5]. Some of the alternative desulfurization approaches which have been previously investigated include oxidative desulfurization, extractive desulfurization, adsorptive desulfurization and biodesulfurization. One common advantage of these processes over the conventional HDS is that these can be conducted at comparatively less severe conditions [1,5–7].

Desulfurization via solvent extraction is a preferable alternative since this process does not usually require additional reagents viz. hydrogen or oxidizing agents thereby reducing the operating cost; the solvents can be regenerated and recycled and additionally the properties of the fuel mixture mostly remain unaltered [2,5,7].

Thus, it is necessary to explore the possibilities of utilizing ecofriendly solvents for extractive desulfurization process featuring good extraction capacity, high selectivity towards the sulfur compounds, easy regeneration, low volatility and viscosity, and high thermal stability. Two emerging classes of environment friendly solvents which have exhibited fuel desulfurization capacities are ionic liquids (ILs) and deep eutectic solvents (DESs). ILs satisfy the criteria of good ecofriendly solvents and their highly tunable nature are suitable for extractive fuel desulfurization [2,8]. ILs though a class of green solvents, possess certain drawbacks viz. high raw material cost and complex synthesis and purification steps involved in their production. DESs overcomes these drawbacks since these are easy to formulate, utilizes cheaper raw materials and there are no byproducts formed thus eliminating the need for further purification. DESs are formed by simply mixing a hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) and a hydrogen bond donor (HBD) at a specific molar ratio. The freezing point of the resulting mixture is much lower than the freezing point of either the HBA or HBD. There are several HBAs and HBDs available therefore numerous DESs having variable properties can be prepared. Thus, it is important to select the HBA and HBD precisely to suit a specific application [4,6,8]. The selection of DES components can be accomplished either by reports published in literature pertaining to the specific application or through machine learning tools like Conditional Generative Adversarial Network (CGAN), machine learning models utilizing multilayer perceptron and support vector regression [9,10].

Some applications of DESs are as a green reaction media, electrolyte in electrochemistry, porous material synthesis media, as catalyst and as a solvent in different extraction processes [1,5]. In recent years, DESs have seen application in crude oil derived fuel processing including dearomatization, denitrogenation and desulfurization [5].

The tetrapropyl ammonium bromide and acetic acid based deep eutectic solvent was utilized by Tarek Lemaoui et. al., for simultaneous dearomatization, desulfurization and denitrogenation of model diesel, attaining efficiencies of approximately 100%, 68% and 89 % respectively [11].

In another investigation conducted by Sajith Babu M.K. et. al., a similar integrated impurity removal from model diesel was performed using a DES consisting of imidazole and sesamol. Extraction efficiencies of nearly100%, 71.1% and 56.1% for desulfurization, dearomatization and denitrogenation respectively after single treatment were achieved [12].

In this investigation, the selection of HBA and HBD was accom- plished based on the review of literature. Among the different HBAs available, choline chloride stands out because it is a class of quaternary ammonium salt (which has been utilized for DES formulation in prior investigations), is readily available, cheap and biodegradable [13–15]. Choline chloride as the HBA also provides the integral melting point depression, which is required for the formation of a DES, due to its low enthalpy of fusion (4.3 KJ/mol). The lower intermolecular interaction tendency of ChCl also leads to lower viscosity of DES which is expected to facilitate higher mass transfer between phases in liquid-liquid extraction [16,17].

Glycerol a non-toxic byproduct from biodiesel production, is a suit- able HBD for a quaternary ammonium salt based DES since it can form good hydrogen bond with choline chloride [1,17,18]. Additionally, when glycerol is used as the HBD, it inhibits the hydrogen bond inter- action among the glycerol molecules, resulting in overall decrease in viscosity of the DES. The investigation conducted by the National Institute of Standards and Technology of the United States showed that when ChCl and glycerol were used as the HBA and HBD respectively, the choline ions entered the hydrogen bond network gaps between the glycerol molecules resulting in "isolation effect" thereby reducing the
viscosity of the system. Reduction in viscosity leads to efficient inter- facial mass transfer [19].
The HBA (choline chloride) and HBD (glycerol) selected for the present investigation forms DES when mixed in the molar ratio of 1:2, as also reported by earlier investigators [4].

The desulfurization efficiency of a DES can be enhanced by incorporating a metal chloride, as a results of π-complex formation between the empty orbital of metals and the un-bonded electron pairs of sulfur [1,20,21].

The work pursued by Zhang, Li.C., et al., indicated that the desulfurization performance for model fuel utilizing metal chlorides based DES followed the order FeCl₃ > ZnCl₂ > CuCl₂ which was attributed to the size of electron cloud distribution of the respective metal ions. The Fe³⁺ ion having the largest electron cloud, could interact readily with the sulfur compounds resulting in the best performance [20].

In another investigation by Shirazinia, S.R., et al., SnCl2, CuCl2, FeCl3, ZnCl2 based DESs were used for extractive desulfurization of fuel. The desulfurization efficiencies of the metal chlorides followed the order SnCl2 > CuCl2 > FeCl3 > ZnCl2. The highest desulfurization perfor- mance of SnCl2 based DES was ascribed to Sn, which being a soft post transition metal does not form a strong complex with the components of DES, thereby can interact more readily with the sulfur compounds giv- ing rise to a high desulfurization efficiency [1].

In this investigation, a DES comprised of choline chloride and glyc-erol has been formulated and modified with four different metal chlo-rides viz. iron(III) chloride, copper(II) chloride, zinc(II) chloride and tin (II) chloride to form novel metal chloride based DESs (MCDESs), with an objective to desulfurize model jet fuel. The MCDESs have been charac-terized by Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), rheology and interfacial surface tension. The Kamlet-Taft (K-T) parameters of the MCDESs were measured and reported for the first time to predict the desulfurization behaviour of the solvents. The effect of different metal chlorides and their varying concentrations in the synthesized DESs on the desulfurization efficiency of model jet fuel was explored to choose the best MCDES. Desulfurization of jet fuel utilizing MCDESs has not been reported by earlier investigators. The effect of different operating parameters on extractive desulfurization was optimized using Analysis of Variance (ANOVA). Additionally, geometry optimization using Ma-terials Studio software version 5.5.2 was also performed for the first time, to predict the affinity of each of the components of the MCDESs towards the sulfur compounds in the model jet fuel desulfurization.

## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. Materials Choline chloride (≥98%) (ChCl), glycerol (≥98%), ferric chloride (98%) (FeCl3), copper chloride (98%) (CuCl2), tin chloride (≥97%) (SnCl2) and zinc chloride (97%) (ZnCl2) were utilized for the preparation of MCDESs. n-decane(≥99%), tolune (99%), n-butane thiol (99.99 %) (thiol) and 1-benzothiophene (≥99%) (BT) were used to formulate the model jet fuel. N,N-diethyl-4nitro aniline, 4-nitro aniline and Nile red dyes were employed for the determination of Kamlet-Taft parameters. Mohr's salt (≥83%) ((NH4)2Fe(SO4)2·6H2O), potassium dichromate (≥96 %) (K2Cr2O7), ferroin indicator, mercury sulphate (≥98%) (HgSO4), silver sulphate (≥99%) (Ag2SO4), sulphuric acid (≥98%) (H2SO4), manganese sulphate monohydrate (≥87%) (MnSO4·H2O), sodium azide (≥98%) (NaN3), potassium iodide (≥98%) (KI), potassium hydroxide (≥87%) (KOH), phosphoric acid (H3PO4), magnesium sulphate (≥98%) (MgSO4), calcium chloride (≥99%) (CaCl2) were used to evaluate the biodegradability of MCDES. All the reagents were procured from Merck Specialities Pvt. Ltd., and were used as received.

## 2.2. Methods ### 2.2.1. Formulation of MCDES The reagents utilized in DESs formulation, viz. ChCl, glycerol and the metal chlorides are hygroscopic in nature therefore each of these were dried in a vacuum dryer for 10 h at 70 °C and 400 mmHg pressure prior to preparation. A basic DES was prepared by combining choline chloride and glycerol in a 1:2 M ratio and this mixture was stirred for 3 h at 80 °C resulting in the formation of a clear liquid. To this DES, varying concentrations of metal chlorides were added and stirring was continued at the same temperature for further 2 h until a clear homogenous solution was obtained. The composition of the formulated MCDESs are presented in Table 1. Although higher concentration of zinc chloride and tin chloride formed homogenous mixtures initially, but upon being cooled (25 °C), resulted in precipitation, thus these mixtures were not utilized for further investigation. The precipitation in these cases might be due to the lower solubility of these metal salts in the choline chloride based DES.

2.2.2. _Characterization of the formulated MCDESs_ The MCDESs were characterized using FTIR, rheology and interfacial surface tension. FTIR characterization was performed using Spectrum 100 FTIR instrument of Perkin Elmer with a wavelength range of 4000–450 cm⁻¹ to determine the bond structure in MCDESs as well as the alteration in different molecular bonding ensuing desulfurization. In order to perform FTIR of the liquid samples, these were immobilized on IR grade KBr and pelletized.
Rotational viscometer ViscoQC 300-L of Anton Parr GmbH, Austria equipped with the bob and cup arrangement (DG26 spindle) was used to
determine the dynamic viscosities of the MCDESs and the model jet fuel at a temperature of 25 °C.
The interfacial surface tension of the different MCDESs and model fuel interface was measured using the Du Nuoy, Testmaster tensiometer of Testing Instruments at a temperature of 25 °C.

The Kamlet–Taft solvatochromic (K-T) parameters of the MCDESs were determined from the maxima UV-vis absorption peaks of the solutions of three dyes (N,N-diethyl-4-nitroaniline, 4-nitroaniline, and Nile red). These parameters were used to quantify the hydrogen-bond donating ability (α), the hydrogen bond accepting ability (β) and polarity/polarizability (π*) of MCDESs utilizing the respective dyes. A high β value might have a direct effect on the desulfurization capacity of the DES through the formation of hydrogen bonding with the lone pair of sulfur. While a high π* indicates better stability of the DES liquid which could enable better recycling capacity [22–25]. Eqs. 1–4 were used to evaluate these parameters.

2.2.3. *Molecular dynamic simulation* Geometry optimization of the MCDESs and model jet fuel components were performed by the DMol3 module of Materials Studio5.5.2. The optimization parameters which were utilized are, Meta-Generalized Gradient Approximation (m-GGA) and Molecular Out-of-distribution Generalization-1 (MOG-1) functionals along with Double Zeta with Polarization (DNP) as the basis set. The maximum force, maximum displacement, maximum iteration, maximum step size, SCF tolerance, maximum SCF cycle, multipolar expansion, spin, were 0.004Ha/Å, 0.005 Å, 1000, 0.3 Å, 0.2, 1000, hexadecapole and 0.5 respectively.
These calculations yielded the sigma profiles of the components of the solvents as well as the model fuel, which were analysed to get an insight of the desulfurization process [28–30].

2.2.4. Model jet fuel preparation and desulfurization process The model jet fuel was prepared by combining n-decane and toluene in a volumetric ratio of 4:1 and the sulfur compounds (thiol and BT) were added to this mixture at a concentration of 5000 ppm on elemental sulfur basis. Each of the MCDESs was mixed with the model jet fuel in the ratio of 1:5 (v/v) and agitated using magnetic stirrer at 400 rpm maintaining a temperature of 25 °C. Samples of the treated model fuel were collected at the end of 3 h. The sulfur content after desulfurization was analysed using Trace 1300 Gas Chromatograph (GC) by Thermo Fischer Scientific Inc., USA equipped with TR-5 GC capillary column having an internal diameter of 0.32 mm, length of 30 m and a film thickness of 1 × 10-2 mm and a flame ionization detector (FID). The flow rate of carrier gas (nitrogen) was maintained at 1.5 ml/min. All the experiments were carried out in triplicate and the average value was reported.
The desulfurization efficiency was determined using the following eq. (9):
Percentage desulfurization = $\frac{I - F}{I}$ \times 100% (9)
where, I denotes the initial concentration (ppm) on elemental sulfur basis.
F denotes the final concentration (ppm) on elemental sulfur basis.

### 2.2.5. Optimization of desulfurization process Design Expert 8.5 software was used for process optimization using the Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) for the accuracy evaluation of the liquid-liquid extraction process. A three-factor-two-level Central Composite Design (CCD) was used to optimize the extraction conditions. Based on the experimental factors solvent to feed ratio (A), concentration of metal chloride in MCDES (mole ratio) (B), and extraction time (min.) (C) were chosen as independent variables in CCD and tested in a 20-run experiments (with 7 central point runs). Each independent variable was coded at two levels, -1 and + 1, for low and high levels, respectively and is represented in Table 2 [31].

2.2.6. _Error analysis_ The error analysis is required for evaluating the accuracy the liquid- liquid extraction process. The error range (approximately 0.05 %) for the experiments performed in triplicates are depicted as error bars in the respective plots [32,33].

2.2.7. *Regeneration and reusability of solvent* The used MCDES (CuDES0.5) was regenerated by dissolving in water to separate out the absorbed sulfur compounds as raffinate (top layer). The aqueous solution of MCDES was then collected and the water was removed by rotary vacuum evaporation at a temperature of 70 °C [4].

## 3. Results and discussions ### 3.1. FTIR characterization Fig. 1 represents the FTIR of the MCDESS (FeDES0.05, CuDES0.05, SnDES0.05 and ZnDES0.05) before and after desulfurization. The peak at 3393.59 cm⁻¹ is attributed to the asymmetric N—H stretching of ChCl [29]. This peak might have overlapped the O—H stretching peak for glycerol which lies at 3265 cm⁻¹ [12]. The O—H bond stretching of ChCl is depicted by the peaks lying in the range of 3000-2900 cm⁻¹ [1,34]. Another peak pertaining to the C—H stretching in glycerol is present in the wave number range of 2943-2873 cm⁻¹ in all the FTIR spectra [34]. The presence of the peaks of glycerol and ChCl in the unused MCDESS signify that no reaction has occurred between the HBA and HBD of the unused MCDESs. The peak at 1653.66 cm⁻¹ which corresponds to the C=O stretching vibration might be attributed to the presence of trace amounts of esters in the glycerol used for DES formulation [35,36]. Another peak pertaining to the CH₃ and CH₂ rocking vibration in ChCl at 1479.58 cm⁻¹ is also observed in all the spectra for the unused solvent [37]. The C—O stretching vibration for glycerol is depicted by the peak at 1209.11 cm⁻¹ [35]. The C—N stretching vibration of ChCl is indicated by the peak at 1058 cm⁻¹ [38]. The peak at 923 cm⁻¹ is assigned to the symmetric C—N stretching of ChCl [39].
The peaks lying in the range of 750-450 cm⁻¹ exhibit the presence of metal chlorides in the MCDESs. These peaks for the metal chlorides are attributed to the M-Cl bond stretching vibrations [1,40].

The peak widening at 3393.59 cm⁻¹ after desulfurization in case of all the solvents indicate that desulfurization mainly takes place through hydrogen bonding between the sulfur impurities and the components of the MCDESS [20]. The peak at 3024.19 cm⁻¹ pertaining to the CH₃ out of plane stretching of thiol is the most prominent in case of used CuDES which signifies that this particular solvent might be most selective in removing thiol [41]. It is also noted that in the case of CuDESU (Fig. 1 (b)) there was a significant elongation in the peak at 1653.66 cm⁻¹ which suggested that the Cu²⁺ ion in CuDES can form π-π complexion with the aromatic ring of BT [20].The elongation of the peaks at 1479.58 cm⁻¹ denotes the C=C stretching of aromatic ring probably due to the presence of BT in the used MCDESSs [42]. The peak values lying within 1276.91 to 1209.08 cm⁻¹ that correspond to the bending atomic motions of the thiophenic ring of BT, also exhibit the existence of this compound in the used MCDESS [43].

## 3.2. Rheology analysis of the MCDESSs The Table 3 lists the viscosities of the MCDESs and model fuel. For the MCDESs, it is observed that the values of viscosities are in the order of 10³mPa.s while that of the model fuel is 10⁻¹ mPa.s. Thus the viscosity difference between MCDESs and the model fuel are in the magnitude of 10⁴mPa.s which indicate that the extract and raffinate phases are expected to separate out quickly [44,45].

3.3. *Determination of the surface tension of the model fuel-MCDES interface* In a liquid-liquid extraction system the interfacial surface tension plays a crucial role in mass transfer between the two phases and a low surface tension is preferable. However, a very low interfacial surface tension is not desirable since this condition requires longer time for phase separation at the end of the extraction cycle and can also lead to emulsification [46]. It is observed that the values of interfacial surface tension between the MCDESs and model jet fuel phases lie in the order of 10-2 N/m, which imply that the dispersed phases will coalesce rapidly (within 5 min) thereby keeping the equilibrium holdup time to a minimum [44]. 3.4. *Estimation of Kamlet-Taft solvatochromic parameters of the MCDESs*

The Kamlet-Taft solvochromic parameters pertaining to HBD ability (α), HBA ability (β) and polarizability (π*) of the MCDESs are reported in Table 5. It is observed that α and β values of CuDES0.5 are the highest which indicates best solvent stability. In case of thiol, it is observed that a major peak is present in the negative side of the non-bonding region, signifying that it is also non-polar in nature. ## 3.8. Desulfurization performance analysis of the MCDESS Fig. 6. depicts the desulfurization performance of the MCDESs towards the model jet fuel after a treatment time of 3 h. From the plot it is evident that for the metal chlorides used, desulfurization performance follows the trend CuCl₂ > FeCl₃ > SnCl₂ > ZnCl₂. This result is in accordance with the sigma profile analysis of the MCDESs. The higher hydrogen bond forming tendency of CuDES with both thiol and BT, compared to the other MCDESs as is evident from the FTIR of the used MCDESs implies that more sulfur compounds get extracted by this solvent. It is also observed that the desulfurization tendency of copper based DESs varies as CuDES0.5 > CuDES0.35 > CuDES0.2 > CuDES0.05. This could be attributed to the high interaction capacity of the Cu²⁺ ion with the respective sulfur compounds as inferred from the molecular dynamic investigation. It is also evident from the β value of K-T parameters that CuDES0.5 possess the highest HBA ability which might be responsible for the best desulfurization performance by this MCDES. On the other hand in case of the iron based DES, the trend of desulfurization is as follows FeDES0.5 > FEDESO.2 > FeDES0.05 > FeDES0.35.

The extracted sulfur compounds might be used as industrial raw materials or treated with caustic solution to produce sulphites and hy- drocarbons thereby converting them into value added products [4].

A further desulfurization investigation on the basis of total sulfur in the model jet has been carried out in the case of CuDES0.5, to get an insight into the desulfurization process which is depicted in Fig. 7. The desulfurization capacity of this particular solvent is 56.02% after 30 min of extraction which steadily increases to 99.15% at the end of 3 h. ## 4. Conclusions In this present investigation, four metal chlorides incorporated DESs have been formulated and their efficiency towards model jet fuel desulfurization was studied. The characterization of CuDES0.5 by HNMR indicated the presence of good hydrogen bonding in this MCDES validating the formation of DES structure. The FTIR analysis of MCDESs revealed that the desulfurization phenomenon occurred through hydrogen bond formation between the MCDESs and the sulfur compounds as well as by π-πcomplexion of the sulfur compounds with the

metal ions. The effect of hydrogen bond on desulfurization performance was also revealed from the K-T parameters which indicated that CuDES 0.5 has the greatest HBA ability, which can be attributed to its highest desulfurization efficiency. Further characterization of the MCDESs by interfacial surface tension and rheology implied that the extract and raffinate phases are expected to separate out quickly minimizing the holdup time for phase separation. Additionally, the comparative analysis of the sigma profiles of the model sulfur compounds as well as the components of the MCDESs as obtained from the DMol3 module of Materials Studio 5.5.2 has indicated that the CuDES has higher interaction ability with the sulfur compounds under consideration resulting in higher desulfurization efficiency. Model jet fuel desulfurization analysis was performed with the MCDESs at a temperature of 25 °C and the results were in accordance to the predictions from FTIR and molecular dynamic simulation indicating that, CuDES has the highest separation efficiency. Among the CuDESs prepared, CuDES0.50 (ChCl: glycerol:CuCl2 molar ratio of 1:2:0.50) yielded the highest desulfurization efficiency (99.15 % on total sulfur basis) for a solvent:feed ratio of 1:5 and an extraction time of 3 h. The process of desulfurization was optimized by ANOVA which indicated that the optimum values of solvent: feed ratio, concentration of CuCl2 in MCDES and extraction time are 35.72, 1.07 (mole ratio) and 82.50 min respectively. Again, in this investigation, the low amount of MCDESs utilized (1:5 volumetric ratio of solvent:model jet fuel) for this extractive desulfurization along with good regeneration ability of CuDES0.5 can contribute towards the economic viability of this process. The solvent CuDES0.5 also showed good biodegradability behaviour which manifests that this is an eco-friendly solvent.

Journal of Molecular Liquids 437 (2025) 128529 <::logo: Elsevier NON SOLLUS A detailed illustration of a person and a tree, with the word "ELSEVIER" in orange below it.::> Contents lists available at ScienceDirect Journal of Molecular Liquids journal homepage: www.elsevier.com/locate/molliq <::logo: Elsevier Elsevier logo A square logo with the stylized letter "E" and a small bird icon within a white square.::> Extractive desulfurization of model jet fuel using metal chloride modified deep eutectic solvents Rupam Chatterjee a, Debarati Mitra a,* a Department of Chemical Technology, University of Calcutta, Kolkata 700009, India ARTICLE INFO --- Keywords: Model jet fuel Desulfurization Deep eutectic solvents Solvent extraction Molecular dynamic simulation ABSTRACT Crude oil contains various organic sulfur compounds comprising of heterocyclic and paraffinic hydrocarbons. During upgradation of crude oil, these sulfur compounds inevitably end up in the final products, which include different fuel fractions (gasoline, kerosene, diesel, etc.). Jet fuels are one such crude oil fraction. Combustion of high sulfur containing fuels lead to sulfur oxide emissions which is detrimental for the environment. Hydrodesulfurization (HDS) process is the conventional fuel desulfurization approach. However, this method is cost and energy intensive therefore, alternative desulfurization approaches are continually being investigated. One such fuel desulfurization route is solvent extraction utilizing deep eutectic solvents (DESs). In this investigation, a choline chloride and glycerol based DES has been formulated. Four different metal chlorides viz. iron(III) chloride, copper(II) chloride, zinc(II) chloride and tin(II) chloride were added to the DES with an objective to enhance the desulfurization efficiency. These solvents were characterized by FTIR, rheology, surface tension and Kamlet-Taft parameters. The effectiveness of these solvents towards desulfurization of model jet fuel has been analysed. A molecular dynamic simulation of the solvents as well as the model fuel has also been carried out for better understanding of the desulfurization process. Both the experimental and simulated findings indicated that the desulfurization efficiency of the DES containing copper(II) chloride was the maximum. The highest desulfurization efficiency of 99.15% (on total sulfur basis) with a solvent:feed ratio of 1:5 at an operating temperature of 25 °C and an extraction time of 3 h was achieved using the aforementioned DES. 1. Introduction Organic sulfur compounds are an integral part of petroleum distillates, including fuels. Jet fuel is no exception and untreated jet fuel can contain as high as 10,000 ppm of sulfur. Sulfur laden fuels when combusted in engines, lead to the emission of sulfur oxides (SOx), which eventually causes environmental pollution. Some of the undesirable effects of SOx pollution include acid rain, formation of obnoxious smog which can cause severe respiratory and cardiovascular problems in humans [1]. This has necessitated stringent measures from regulatory bodies all over the world to reduce the sulfur content in fuels, below a certain threshold [2]. In the case of jet fuels, the maximum permissible limit of sulfur is 3000 ppm since most of the emissions from jet fuel occur at high altitudes which have low impact on the environment. However, some of the jet emissions at lower altitudes, especially near airports could have detrimental effects. Also, this high sulfur content in jet fuels make them unsuitable for alternative applications viz. in fuel cells [3]. Hydrodesulfurization (HDS) utilizing NiMo/CoMo catalysts is the stereotypical fuel desulfurization approach in refineries [4]. However, this process operates under high pressure and high temperature and utilizes expensive proprietary catalysts making itboth energy and cost intensive. Also, HDS process is not very efficient in removing hetero- cyclic sulfur compounds under standard operating conditions due to low reactivity of these compounds and higher severity (i.e. higher temper- ature and pressure) is required to remove these compounds [1,2,4,5]. Some of the alternative desulfurization approaches which have been previously investigated include oxidative desulfurization, extractive desulfurization, adsorptive desulfurization and biodesulfurization. One common advantage of these processes over the conventional HDS is that these can be conducted at comparatively less severe conditions [1,5–7]. Desulfurization via solvent extraction is a preferable alternative since this process does not usually require additional reagents viz. hydrogen or oxidizing agents thereby reducing the operating cost; the solvents can be regenerated and recycled and additionally the properties of the fuel mixture mostly remain unaltered [2,5,7]. Thus, it is necessary to explore the possibilities of utilizing ecofriendly solvents for extractive desulfurization process featuring good extraction capacity, high selectivity towards the sulfur compounds, easy regeneration, low volatility and viscosity, and high thermal stability. Two emerging classes of environment friendly solvents which have exhibited fuel desulfurization capacities are ionic liquids (ILs) and deep eutectic solvents (DESs). ILs satisfy the criteria of good ecofriendly solvents and their highly tunable nature are suitable for extractive fuel desulfurization [2,8]. ILs though a class of green solvents, possess certain drawbacks viz. high raw material cost and complex synthesis and purification steps involved in their production. DESs overcomes these drawbacks since these are easy to formulate, utilizes cheaper raw materials and there are no byproducts formed thus eliminating the need for further purification. DESs are formed by simply mixing a hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) and a hydrogen bond donor (HBD) at a specific molar ratio. The freezing point of the resulting mixture is much lower than the freezing point of either the HBA or HBD. There are several HBAs and HBDs available therefore numerous DESs having variable properties can be prepared. Thus, it is important to select the HBA and HBD precisely to suit a specific application [4,6,8]. The selection of DES components can be accomplished either by reports published in literature pertaining to the specific application or through machine learning tools like Conditional Generative Adversarial Network (CGAN), machine learning models utilizing multilayer perceptron and support vector regression [9,10]. Some applications of DESs are as a green reaction media, electrolyte in electrochemistry, porous material synthesis media, as catalyst and as a solvent in different extraction processes [1,5]. In recent years, DESs have seen application in crude oil derived fuel processing including dearomatization, denitrogenation and desulfurization [5]. The tetrapropyl ammonium bromide and acetic acid based deep eutectic solvent was utilized by Tarek Lemaoui et. al., for simultaneous dearomatization, desulfurization and denitrogenation of model diesel, attaining efficiencies of approximately 100%, 68% and 89 % respectively [11]. In another investigation conducted by Sajith Babu M.K. et. al., a similar integrated impurity removal from model diesel was performed using a DES consisting of imidazole and sesamol. Extraction efficiencies of nearly100%, 71.1% and 56.1% for desulfurization, dearomatization and denitrogenation respectively after single treatment were achieved [12]. In this investigation, the selection of HBA and HBD was accom- plished based on the review of literature. Among the different HBAs available, choline chloride stands out because it is a class of quaternary ammonium salt (which has been utilized for DES formulation in prior investigations), is readily available, cheap and biodegradable [13–15]. Choline chloride as the HBA also provides the integral melting point depression, which is required for the formation of a DES, due to its low enthalpy of fusion (4.3 KJ/mol). The lower intermolecular interaction tendency of ChCl also leads to lower viscosity of DES which is expected to facilitate higher mass transfer between phases in liquid-liquid extraction [16,17]. Glycerol a non-toxic byproduct from biodiesel production, is a suit- able HBD for a quaternary ammonium salt based DES since it can form good hydrogen bond with choline chloride [1,17,18]. Additionally, when glycerol is used as the HBD, it inhibits the hydrogen bond inter- action among the glycerol molecules, resulting in overall decrease in viscosity of the DES. The investigation conducted by the National Institute of Standards and Technology of the United States showed that when ChCl and glycerol were used as the HBA and HBD respectively, the choline ions entered the hydrogen bond network gaps between the glycerol molecules resulting in "isolation effect" thereby reducing the viscosity of the system. Reduction in viscosity leads to efficient inter- facial mass transfer [19]. The HBA (choline chloride) and HBD (glycerol) selected for the present investigation forms DES when mixed in the molar ratio of 1:2, as also reported by earlier investigators [4]. The desulfurization efficiency of a DES can be enhanced by incorporating a metal chloride, as a results of π-complex formation between the empty orbital of metals and the un-bonded electron pairs of sulfur [1,20,21]. The work pursued by Zhang, Li.C., et al., indicated that the desulfurization performance for model fuel utilizing metal chlorides based DES followed the order FeCl₃ > ZnCl₂ > CuCl₂ which was attributed to the size of electron cloud distribution of the respective metal ions. The Fe³⁺ ion having the largest electron cloud, could interact readily with the sulfur compounds resulting in the best performance [20]. In another investigation by Shirazinia, S.R., et al., SnCl2, CuCl2, FeCl3, ZnCl2 based DESs were used for extractive desulfurization of fuel. The desulfurization efficiencies of the metal chlorides followed the order SnCl2 > CuCl2 > FeCl3 > ZnCl2. The highest desulfurization perfor- mance of SnCl2 based DES was ascribed to Sn, which being a soft post transition metal does not form a strong complex with the components of DES, thereby can interact more readily with the sulfur compounds giv- ing rise to a high desulfurization efficiency [1]. In this investigation, a DES comprised of choline chloride and glyc-erol has been formulated and modified with four different metal chlo-rides viz. iron(III) chloride, copper(II) chloride, zinc(II) chloride and tin (II) chloride to form novel metal chloride based DESs (MCDESs), with an objective to desulfurize model jet fuel. The MCDESs have been charac-terized by Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), rheology and interfacial surface tension. The Kamlet-Taft (K-T) parameters of the MCDESs were measured and reported for the first time to predict the desulfurization behaviour of the solvents. The effect of different metal chlorides and their varying concentrations in the synthesized DESs on the desulfurization efficiency of model jet fuel was explored to choose the best MCDES. Desulfurization of jet fuel utilizing MCDESs has not been reported by earlier investigators. The effect of different operating parameters on extractive desulfurization was optimized using Analysis of Variance (ANOVA). Additionally, geometry optimization using Ma-terials Studio software version 5.5.2 was also performed for the first time, to predict the affinity of each of the components of the MCDESs towards the sulfur compounds in the model jet fuel desulfurization. ## 2. Materials and methods ### 2.1. N,N-diethyl-4nitro aniline, 4-nitro aniline and Nile red dyes were employed for the determination of Kamlet-Taft parameters. ## 2.2. Methods ### 2.2.1. Formulation of MCDES The reagents utilized in DESs formulation, viz. ChCl, glycerol and the metal chlorides are hygroscopic in nature therefore each of these were dried in a vacuum dryer for 10 h at 70 °C and 400 mmHg pressure prior to preparation. A basic DES was prepared by combining choline chloride and glycerol in a 1:2 M ratio and this mixture was stirred for 3 h at 80 °C resulting in the formation of a clear liquid. To this DES, varying concentrations of metal chlorides were added and stirring was continued at the same temperature for further 2 h until a clear homogenous solution was obtained. The composition of the formulated MCDESs are presented in Table 1. Although higher concentration of zinc chloride and tin chloride formed homogenous mixtures initially, but upon being cooled (25 °C), resulted in precipitation, thus these mixtures were not utilized for further investigation. The precipitation in these cases might be due to the lower solubility of these metal salts in the choline chloride based DES. 2.2.2. _Characterization of the formulated MCDESs_ The MCDESs were characterized using FTIR, rheology and interfacial surface tension. FTIR characterization was performed using Spectrum 100 FTIR instrument of Perkin Elmer with a wavelength range of 4000–450 cm⁻¹ to determine the bond structure in MCDESs as well as the alteration in different molecular bonding ensuing desulfurization. In order to perform FTIR of the liquid samples, these were immobilized on IR grade KBr and pelletized. Rotational viscometer ViscoQC 300-L of Anton Parr GmbH, Austria equipped with the bob and cup arrangement (DG26 spindle) was used to determine the dynamic viscosities of the MCDESs and the model jet fuel at a temperature of 25 °C. The interfacial surface tension of the different MCDESs and model fuel interface was measured using the Du Nuoy, Testmaster tensiometer of Testing Instruments at a temperature of 25 °C. Conclusions In this present investigation, four metal chlorides incorporated DESs have been formulated and their efficiency towards model jet fuel desulfurization was studied. The characterization of CuDES0.5 by HNMR indicated the presence of good hydrogen bonding in this MCDES validating the formation of DES structure. The FTIR analysis of MCDESs revealed that the desulfurization phenomenon occurred through hydrogen bond formation between the MCDESs and the sulfur compounds as well as by π-πcomplexion of the sulfur compounds with the metal ions. The effect of hydrogen bond on desulfurization performance was also revealed from the K-T parameters which indicated that CuDES 0.5 has the greatest HBA ability, which can be attributed to its highest desulfurization efficiency. Further characterization of the MCDESs by interfacial surface tension and rheology implied that the extract and raffinate phases are expected to separate out quickly minimizing the holdup time for phase separation. Additionally, the comparative analysis of the sigma profiles of the model sulfur compounds as well as the components of the MCDESs as obtained from the DMol3 module of Materials Studio 5.5.2 has indicated that the CuDES has higher interaction ability with the sulfur compounds under consideration resulting in higher desulfurization efficiency. Model jet fuel desulfurization analysis was performed with the MCDESs at a temperature of 25 °C and the results were in accordance to the predictions from FTIR and molecular dynamic simulation indicating that, CuDES has the highest separation efficiency. Among the CuDESs prepared, CuDES0.50 (ChCl: glycerol:CuCl2 molar ratio of 1:2:0.50) yielded the highest desulfurization efficiency (99.15 % on total sulfur basis) for a solvent:feed ratio of 1:5 and an extraction time of 3 h. The process of desulfurization was optimized by ANOVA which indicated that the optimum values of solvent: feed ratio, concentration of CuCl2 in MCDES and extraction time are 35.72, 1.07 (mole ratio) and 82.50 min respectively. Again, in this investigation, the low amount of MCDESs utilized (1:5 volumetric ratio of solvent:model jet fuel) for this extractive desulfurization along with good regeneration ability of CuDES0.5 can contribute towards the economic viability of this process. The solvent CuDES0.5 also showed good biodegradability behaviour which manifests that this is an eco-friendly solvent. During upgradation of crude oil, these sulfur compounds inevitably end up in the final products, which include different fuel fractions (gasoline, kerosene, diesel, etc.). Jet fuels are one such crude oil fraction. Combustion of high sulfur containing fuels lead to sulfur oxide emissions which is detrimental for the environment. Hydrodesulfurization (HDS) process is the conventional fuel desulfurization approach. However, this method is cost and energy intensive therefore, alternative desulfurization approaches are continually being investigated. One such fuel desulfurization route is solvent extraction utilizing deep eutectic solvents (DESs). In this investigation, a choline chloride and glycerol based DES has been formulated. Four different metal chlorides viz. iron(III) chloride, copper(II) chloride, zinc(II) chloride and tin(II) chloride were added to the DES with an objective to enhance the desulfurization efficiency. These solvents were characterized by FTIR, rheology, surface tension and Kamlet-Taft parameters. The effectiveness of these solvents towards desulfurization of model jet fuel has been analysed. A molecular dynamic simulation of the solvents as well as the model fuel has also been carried out for better understanding of the desulfurization process. Both the experimental and simulated findings indicated that the desulfurization efficiency of the DES containing copper(II) chloride was the maximum. The highest desulfurization efficiency of 99.15% (on total sulfur basis) with a solvent:feed ratio of 1:5 at an operating temperature of 25 °C and an extraction time of 3 h was achieved using the aforementioned DES. 1. Introduction Organic sulfur compounds are an integral part of petroleum distillates, including fuels. Jet fuel is no exception and untreated jet fuel can contain as high as 10,000 ppm of sulfur. Sulfur laden fuels when combusted in engines, lead to the emission of sulfur oxides (SOx), which eventually causes environmental pollution. Some of the undesirable effects of SOx pollution include acid rain, formation of obnoxious smog which can cause severe respiratory and cardiovascular problems in humans [1]. This has necessitated stringent measures from regulatory bodies all over the world to reduce the sulfur content in fuels, below a certain threshold [2]. In the case of jet fuels, the maximum permissible limit of sulfur is 3000 ppm since most of the emissions from jet fuel occur at high altitudes which have low impact on the environment. However, some of the jet emissions at lower altitudes, especially near airports could have detrimental effects. Also, this high sulfur content in jet fuels make them unsuitable for alternative applications viz. in fuel cells [3]. Hydrodesulfurization (HDS) utilizing NiMo/CoMo catalysts is the stereotypical fuel desulfurization approach in refineries [4]. However, this process operates under high pressure and high temperature and utilizes expensive proprietary catalysts making itboth energy and cost intensive. Also, HDS process is not very efficient in removing hetero- cyclic sulfur compounds under standard operating conditions due to low reactivity of these compounds and higher severity (i.e. higher temper- ature and pressure) is required to remove these compounds [1,2,4,5]. Some of the alternative desulfurization approaches which have been previously investigated include oxidative desulfurization, extractive desulfurization, adsorptive desulfurization and biodesulfurization. One common advantage of these processes over the conventional HDS is that these can be conducted at comparatively less severe conditions [1,5–7]. Desulfurization via solvent extraction is a preferable alternative since this process does not usually require additional reagents viz. hydrogen or oxidizing agents thereby reducing the operating cost; the solvents can be regenerated and recycled and additionally the properties of the fuel mixture mostly remain unaltered [2,5,7]. Thus, it is necessary to explore the possibilities of utilizing ecofriendly solvents for extractive desulfurization process featuring good extraction capacity, high selectivity towards the sulfur compounds, easy regeneration, low volatility and viscosity, and high thermal stability. Two emerging classes of environment friendly solvents which have exhibited fuel desulfurization capacities are ionic liquids (ILs) and deep eutectic solvents (DESs). ILs satisfy the criteria of good ecofriendly solvents and their highly tunable nature are suitable for extractive fuel desulfurization [2,8]. ILs though a class of green solvents, possess certain drawbacks viz. high raw material cost and complex synthesis and purification steps involved in their production. DESs overcomes these drawbacks since these are easy to formulate, utilizes cheaper raw materials and there are no byproducts formed thus eliminating the need for further purification. DESs are formed by simply mixing a hydrogen bond acceptor (HBA) and a hydrogen bond donor (HBD) at a specific molar ratio. The freezing point of the resulting mixture is much lower than the freezing point of either the HBA or HBD. There are several HBAs and HBDs available therefore numerous DESs having variable properties can be prepared. Thus, it is important to select the HBA and HBD precisely to suit a specific application [4,6,8]. The selection of DES components can be accomplished either by reports published in literature pertaining to the specific application or through machine learning tools like Conditional Generative Adversarial Network (CGAN), machine learning models utilizing multilayer perceptron and support vector regression [9,10]. Some applications of DESs are as a green reaction media, electrolyte in electrochemistry, porous material synthesis media, as catalyst and as a solvent in different extraction processes [1,5]. In recent years, DESs have seen application in crude oil derived fuel processing including dearomatization, denitrogenation and desulfurization [5]. The tetrapropyl ammonium bromide and acetic acid based deep eutectic solvent was utilized by Tarek Lemaoui et. al., for simultaneous dearomatization, desulfurization and denitrogenation of model diesel, attaining efficiencies of approximately 100%, 68% and 89 % respectively [11]. In another investigation conducted by Sajith Babu M.K. et. al., a similar integrated impurity removal from model diesel was performed using a DES consisting of imidazole and sesamol. Extraction efficiencies of nearly100%, 71.1% and 56.1% for desulfurization, dearomatization and denitrogenation respectively after single treatment were achieved [12]. In this investigation, the selection of HBA and HBD was accom- plished based on the review of literature. Among the different HBAs available, choline chloride stands out because it is a class of quaternary ammonium salt (which has been utilized for DES formulation in prior investigations), is readily available, cheap and biodegradable [13–15]. Choline chloride as the HBA also provides the integral melting point depression, which is required for the formation of a DES, due to its low enthalpy of fusion (4.3 KJ/mol). The lower intermolecular interaction tendency of ChCl also leads to lower viscosity of DES which is expected to facilitate higher mass transfer between phases in liquid-liquid extraction [16,17]. Glycerol a non-toxic byproduct from biodiesel production, is a suit- able HBD for a quaternary ammonium salt based DES since it can form good hydrogen bond with choline chloride [1,17,18]. Additionally, when glycerol is used as the HBD, it inhibits the hydrogen bond inter- action among the glycerol molecules, resulting in overall decrease in viscosity of the DES. The investigation conducted by the National Institute of Standards and Technology of the United States showed that when ChCl and glycerol were used as the HBA and HBD respectively, the choline ions entered the hydrogen bond network gaps between the glycerol molecules resulting in "isolation effect" thereby reducing the viscosity of the system. Reduction in viscosity leads to efficient inter- facial mass transfer [19]. The HBA (choline chloride) and HBD (glycerol) selected for the present investigation forms DES when mixed in the molar ratio of 1:2, as also reported by earlier investigators [4]. The desulfurization efficiency of a DES can be enhanced by incorporating a metal chloride, as a results of π-complex formation between the empty orbital of metals and the un-bonded electron pairs of sulfur [1,20,21]. The work pursued by Zhang, Li.C., et al., indicated that the desulfurization performance for model fuel utilizing metal chlorides based DES followed the order FeCl₃ > ZnCl₂ > CuCl₂ which was attributed to the size of electron cloud distribution of the respective metal ions. The Fe³⁺ ion having the largest electron cloud, could interact readily with the sulfur compounds resulting in the best performance [20]. In another investigation by Shirazinia, S.R., et al., SnCl2, CuCl2, FeCl3, ZnCl2 based DESs were used for extractive desulfurization of fuel. The desulfurization efficiencies of the metal chlorides followed the order SnCl2 > CuCl2 > FeCl3 > ZnCl2. The highest desulfurization perfor- mance of SnCl2 based DES was ascribed to Sn, which being a soft post transition metal does not form a strong complex with the components of DES, thereby can interact more readily with the sulfur compounds giv- ing rise to a high desulfurization efficiency [1]. In this investigation, a DES comprised of choline chloride and glyc-erol has been formulated and modified with four different metal chlo-rides viz. iron(III) chloride, copper(II) chloride, zinc(II) chloride and tin (II) chloride to form novel metal chloride based DESs (MCDESs), with an objective to desulfurize model jet fuel. The MCDESs have been charac-terized by Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR), rheology and interfacial surface tension. The Kamlet-Taft (K-T) parameters of the MCDESs were measured and reported for the first time to predict the desulfurization behaviour of the solvents. The effect of different metal chlorides and their varying concentrations in the synthesized DESs on the desulfurization efficiency of model jet fuel was explored to choose the best MCDES. Desulfurization of jet fuel utilizing MCDESs has not been reported by earlier investigators. ## 2.2. Methods ### 2.2.1. Formulation of MCDES The reagents utilized in DESs formulation, viz. ChCl, glycerol and the metal chlorides are hygroscopic in nature therefore each of these were dried in a vacuum dryer for 10 h at 70 °C and 400 mmHg pressure prior to preparation. A basic DES was prepared by combining choline chloride and glycerol in a 1:2 M ratio and this mixture was stirred for 3 h at 80 °C resulting in the formation of a clear liquid. To this DES, varying concentrations of metal chlorides were added and stirring was continued at the same temperature for further 2 h until a clear homogenous solution was obtained. The composition of the formulated MCDESs are presented in Table 1. Although higher concentration of zinc chloride and tin chloride formed homogenous mixtures initially, but upon being cooled (25 °C), resulted in precipitation, thus these mixtures were not utilized for further investigation. The precipitation in these cases might be due to the lower solubility of these metal salts in the choline chloride based DES. 2.2.2. _Characterization of the formulated MCDESs_ The MCDESs were characterized using FTIR, rheology and interfacial surface tension. FTIR characterization was performed using Spectrum 100 FTIR instrument of Perkin Elmer with a wavelength range of 4000–450 cm⁻¹ to determine the bond structure in MCDESs as well as the alteration in different molecular bonding ensuing desulfurization. In order to perform FTIR of the liquid samples, these were immobilized on IR grade KBr and pelletized. Rotational viscometer ViscoQC 300-L of Anton Parr GmbH, Austria equipped with the bob and cup arrangement (DG26 spindle) was used to determine the dynamic viscosities of the MCDESs and the model jet fuel at a temperature of 25 °C. The interfacial surface tension of the different MCDESs and model fuel interface was measured using the Du Nuoy, Testmaster tensiometer of Testing Instruments at a temperature of 25 °C. Conclusions In this present investigation, four metal chlorides incorporated DESs have been formulated and their efficiency towards model jet fuel desulfurization was studied. The characterization of CuDES0.5 by HNMR indicated the presence of good hydrogen bonding in this MCDES validating the formation of DES structure. The FTIR analysis of MCDESs revealed that the desulfurization phenomenon occurred through hydrogen bond formation between the MCDESs and the sulfur compounds as well as by π-πcomplexion of the sulfur compounds with the metal ions. The effect of hydrogen bond on desulfurization performance was also revealed from the K-T parameters which indicated that CuDES 0.5 has the greatest HBA ability, which can be attributed to its highest desulfurization efficiency. Further characterization of the MCDESs by interfacial surface tension and rheology implied that the extract and raffinate phases are expected to separate out quickly minimizing the holdup time for phase separation. Additionally, the comparative analysis of the sigma profiles of the model sulfur compounds as well as the components of the MCDESs as obtained from the DMol3 module of Materials Studio 5.5.2 has indicated that the CuDES has higher interaction ability with the sulfur compounds under consideration resulting in higher desulfurization efficiency. Model jet fuel desulfurization analysis was performed with the MCDESs at a temperature of 25 °C and the results were in accordance to the predictions from FTIR and molecular dynamic simulation indicating that, CuDES has the highest separation efficiency. Among the CuDESs prepared, CuDES0.50 (ChCl: glycerol:CuCl2 molar ratio of 1:2:0.50) yielded the highest desulfurization efficiency (99.15 % on total sulfur basis) for a solvent:feed ratio of 1:5 and an extraction time of 3 h. The process of desulfurization was optimized by ANOVA which indicated that the optimum values of solvent: feed ratio, concentration of CuCl2 in MCDES and extraction time are 35.72, 1.07 (mole ratio) and 82.50 min respectively. Again, in this investigation, the low amount of MCDESs utilized (1:5 volumetric ratio of solvent:model jet fuel) for this extractive desulfurization along with good regeneration ability of CuDES0.5 can contribute towards the economic viability of this process. The solvent CuDES0.5 also showed good biodegradability behaviour which manifests that this is an eco-friendly solvent.
